title: Grüner Veltliner
description: Austria's signature grape: citrus, green apple and a twist of white pepper.
L: Grüner Veltliner, often just Grüner, gives whites with lemon, lime, green apple, pear, green bean, lentil and its signature white pepper. Acidity is medium to high. It ranges from light, crisp everyday wines to powerful, rich ones. It's Austria's most planted grape, about a third of its vineyards.

Grüner Veltliner is native to Austria. DNA shows its parents are Traminer and an old grape found in St. Georgen, near Lake Neusiedl, called St. Georgener-Rebe. Despite its name, it isn't related to Roter Veltliner. It's vigorous and productive, so yield control decides quality.
What is Grüner Veltliner's signature aroma?
A white pepper note sets it apart.

Look for pale lemon, sometimes green-tinged colour, citrus and green apple with white pepper and vegetal notes like green bean, and a crisp, fresh palate. Richer versions add stone fruit, spice and a creamy texture. Compared with Sauvignon Blanc, it's less pungent and more peppery.
Grüner Veltliner is Austria's most planted grape.
Yes, about a third of its vineyards.
Grüner gives citrus, green apple and white pepper
It's Austria's native and most planted grape
Its parents are Traminer and St. Georgener-Rebe

Grüner grows mainly in Niederösterreich, Lower Austria, along the Danube and to the north. Weinviertel, the largest region, makes peppery, fresh Grüner; it was Austria's first DAC, in 2003. The Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal make powerful, structured versions on steep terraces. Vienna also grows it.

Austria's DAC system, Districtus Austriae Controllatus, ties regions to typical grapes and styles. A Weinviertel DAC is Grüner Veltliner; Kamptal DAC and Kremstal DAC are Grüner or Riesling. Labels can add Reserve for riper, fuller wines. The Wachau uses its own terms: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd.
Match each Austrian term to its meaning.
Austria labels by region and style.

Grüner Veltliner is spreading: Slovakia and Czech Republic grow it, and New Zealand, Australia's Adelaide Hills, the US and England have new plantings. Cool to moderate climates suit it best, keeping its freshness and pepper.
A system linking regions to typical grapes and styles
DAC labels tell you region and expected style.

Grüner's white pepper note comes from rotundone, the same compound that gives Syrah its black pepper aroma and is found in peppercorns. It forms in the skins, especially in cooler sites and years. Like in Syrah, about one in five people can't smell it at all.

Grüner grows best on loess, a fine, wind-blown, yellowish silt deposited after the last ice age. Loess is deep, holds water and warms easily, giving full-bodied, rounder Grüner. In the Wachau and Kamptal, loess terraces sit beside primary rock, gneiss and granite, which give leaner, more mineral Grüner, often used for Riesling.
The compound that gives Grüner its white pepper note is ____.
Rotundone, also found in Syrah and peppercorns.

Light Grüner, like many Weinviertel and Steinfeder wines, is crisp, peppery and best young. Powerful Grüner, like Wachau Smaragd or Kamptal Reserve from loess, is rich, with stone fruit, spice and a creamy texture, and can age 10 to 20 years, gaining honey and toast.
Primary rock, not loess, gives leaner wines.
Rotundone gives Grüner its white pepper
Loess gives full, round Grüner; rock gives mineral wines
Styles range from light to powerful and age-worthy

Grüner is famous for being food-friendly. It handles tricky vegetables like asparagus and artichokes, and suits Wiener Schnitzel, a Viennese classic, fried chicken, sushi, Vietnamese and Thai dishes, salads and fresh cheeses. Its pepper suits peppery food.

Serve light Grüner at 7 to 9 degrees, richer styles at 10 to 12. Light styles are best within two years. Smaragd and Reserve can age 10 to 20 years. In Vienna, young Grüner is drunk in Heurigen, wine taverns serving the latest vintage.
Which Viennese dish is a classic match for Grüner?
Breaded veal and Grüner's freshness are a Vienna staple.
Grüner Veltliner is a safe choice at a restaurant when the table orders very different dishes. It rarely clashes.
Yes. It's one of the few wines that does.
Grüner suits schnitzel, asparagus and Asian food
